question: What is the main job of antibiotics in our bodies?

options.A: To treat and manage bacterial infections
options.B: To boost overall red blood cell counts
options.C: To replace lost fluids and electrolytes
options.D: To lower elevated body temperature rapidly

explanation: You got this! Antibiotics are specifically made to hunt down and stop bacteria from causing trouble in the body. They don't touch viruses or fever on their own! [learn more](GNS223_U2_T4#GNS223_U2_T4_h1)

question: When we talk about 'selective toxicity' in pharmacology, what does it mean?

options.A: Effective against only one single species of bacteria
options.B: Safe to give to pregnant women without testing
options.C: Active only when taken on a completely empty stomach
options.D: Harmful to microbes while sparing human cells

explanation: Think of selective toxicity as a smart missile—it attacks the invading germs while leaving your normal body cells safe and sound. Pretty neat, right? [learn more](GNS223_U2_T4#GNS223_U2_T4_h1)

question: How do penicillins primarily kill bacteria?

options.B: Binding directly to human liver enzymes

explanation: Spot on! Penicillins mess up the building blocks of the bacterial cell wall. Without a strong wall, the bacteria burst open and die. [learn more](GNS223_U2_T4#GNS223_U2_T4_h2)

question: What is the big difference between bactericidal and bacteriostatic drugs?

options.A: Bactericidal agents require acidic pH, while bacteriostatic agents need alkaline pH
options.B: Bacteriostatic drugs work only in the lungs, while bactericidal drugs work everywhere
options.C: Bactericidal drugs kill bacteria, whereas bacteriostatic drugs stop their growth
options.D: Bacteriostatic drugs destroy human cells, but bactericidal drugs protect them

explanation: Easy to remember: Bacterici-DAL drugs outright KILL the bacteria, while bacteriostatic drugs just press 'pause' on their growth and let your immune system finish the job! [learn more](GNS223_U2_T4#GNS223_U2_T4_h2)

question: Why do doctors treat tuberculosis (TB) with a mix of several drugs instead of just one?

options.A: To eliminate the need for routine liver function tests
options.B: To prevent the development of drug-resistant strains
options.C: To speed up the patient discharge process immediately
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing drugs

explanation: TB bacteria are clever and mutate easily. Hitting them with multiple drugs at once makes it much harder for them to fight back and become resistant. [learn more](GNS223_U2_T4#GNS223_U2_T4_h3)

question: How do azole antifungal medications mostly work against fungi?

options.A: By blocking bacterial folic acid synthesis
options.B: By stimulating human white blood cell production
options.C: By dissolving the outer viral protein capsule
options.D: By altering fungal cell membrane permeability

explanation: Antifungals poke holes in the fungal cell membrane (by attacking things like ergosterol). This makes all the important cell contents leak out! [learn more](GNS223_U2_T4#GNS223_U2_T4_h3)

question: As a nurse, what is one of the best ways you can help stop drug resistance?

options.A: Administering broad-spectrum drugs for every common viral cold
options.B: Educating patients to finish their entire antibiotic prescription
options.C: Stopping medication immediately once mild symptoms disappear
options.D: Encouraging patients to save leftover pills for future sickness

explanation: You got it! Always remind patients to complete their meds. Stopping early leaves the toughest germs alive to breed stronger, resistant generations. [learn more](GNS223_U2_T4#GNS223_U2_T4_h4)

question: What usually causes antimicrobial resistance to spread in clinical practice?

options.A: Using combination drug therapy for mycobacterial infections
options.B: Regular handwashing and proper cleaning of hospital equipment
options.C: Administering culture-guided targeted therapy to patients
options.D: Inappropriate use and incomplete courses of anti-infective drugs

explanation: Misusing antibiotics—like taking them for viral colds or stopping halfway—teaches bacteria how to survive our best drugs. Good hand hygiene and smart prescribing protect everyone! [learn more](GNS223_U2_T4#GNS223_U2_T4_h4)

question: Why must a nurse collect a wound culture BEFORE giving the first dose of a new antibiotic?

options.A: Starting the drug first will completely destroy all local laboratory equipment
options.B: Laboratory regulations require paperwork to be filed prior to dosing
options.C: Pre-dosing culture collection is only required for oral medications
options.D: The medication can alter bacteria levels and mask the true infection source

explanation: If you give the drug first, it might kill off or hide the bacteria in the sample, giving the lab a false-negative result. Always swab first, treat second! [learn more](GNS223_U2_T4#GNS223_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is the most critical check a nurse must do before giving penicillin for the first time?

options.B: Checking for a history of drug allergies
options.C: Evaluating the patient visual acuity score
options.D: Assessing the patient daily fluid intake

explanation: Safety first! Always check for allergies. A patient with a severe penicillin allergy can crash quickly from anaphylaxis if you miss this step. [learn more](GNS223_U2_T4#GNS223_U2_T4_h5)

question: A patient getting a fast IV infusion of vancomycin suddenly has a red face and neck. What's going on?

options.A: An acute allergic reaction requiring epinephrine
options.B: Severe liver failure due to drug overdose
options.C: Red Man Syndrome caused by infusion rate
options.D: Normal therapeutic effectiveness of the drug

explanation: Classic Red Man Syndrome! It happens when vancomycin goes in too fast and histamine is released. Don't panic—just slow down the infusion rate as ordered. [learn more](GNS223_U2_T4#GNS223_U2_T4_h6)

question: Which body parts must nurses closely monitor for toxicity when a patient is on aminoglycoside antibiotics?
explanation: Remember 'A-E-I-O-U and sometimes Y', but for aminoglycosides, remember Kidneys (nephrotoxicity) and Ears (ototoxicity)! Keep a close eye on urine output and hearing. [learn more](GNS223_U2_T4#GNS223_U2_T4_h6)

question: What key tip should you give a patient who just got a 7-day course of oral antibiotics?

options.A: Share extra pills with family members who catch the same illness
options.B: Finish all 7 days of medicine even if you feel completely better
options.C: Double the next dose if you forget to take one on time
options.D: Stop taking the capsules as soon as your fever goes away

explanation: You're getting the hang of this! Feeling better doesn't mean the germs are all gone. Finish the full 7 days to wipe them out completely. [learn more](GNS223_U2_T4#GNS223_U2_T4_h7)

question: What is the main goal of antimicrobial stewardship programs in hospitals?

options.A: Lowering hospital cleaning budgets by reducing soap purchases
options.B: Optimizing the use of anti-infectives to reduce resistance and harm
options.C: Ensuring every patient receives intravenous drugs automatically
options.D: Eliminating the need for laboratory cultures completely

explanation: Antimicrobial stewardship is all about using the right drug, at the right dose, for the right time—protecting patients from side effects and stopping superbugs from forming. [learn more](GNS223_U2_T4#GNS223_U2_T4_h7)
